title: Interfaces: more than boats to book

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the reservations here, and try your classes from main.

tasks.title: Write Bookable, and a bike shed that is bookable
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1`, write an interface `Bookable` with three methods: `String label()`, `int placesFree()` and `boolean book(int places)`. Then write a class `BikeShed` that implements `Bookable`, with a constructor `BikeShed(int bikes)`. Its label is `Bike shed`. `book` takes the places and gives back `true` while there are enough free; otherwise it changes nothing and gives back `false`.

Check writes a class of its own that implements your `Bookable` with exactly those three methods, and uses it through a variable of type `Bookable`. Then it makes bike sheds, two at once included, keeps them in variables of type `Bookable`, books them down to the last place and one past, and reads what each call gives back.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about writing an interface and implementing one.
Write the interface: three first lines, no bodies.
Write BikeShed: its first line says it implements Bookable, then a field for the places free and the constructor.
Write the three methods with public in front, then take the // off the first lines in main.
hints: An interface lists what a thing can do, not how. BikeShed writes the how.
Every method of an interface is public, so the class must write each one with public in front. book refuses first, then takes the places.
book's shape: `if (places > free) { return false; }`, then `free -= places;` and `return true;`.

tasks.title: Write TourBus, which is bookable and departing
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class `TourBus` that implements both `Bookable` and `Departing`, with a constructor `TourBus(int seats, int hour)`. Its label is `Tour bus`, `book` works as the bike shed's does, and `departsAt` gives back the hour. `Departing` is given above the tasks.

Check runs your class beside a `Bookable` of its own, written as Task 1 asks, so this task is judged on its own lines. It makes tour buses, two at once included, keeps one in a variable of each interface's type, and reads what `label`, `departsAt`, `placesFree` and `book` give back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about one class with two interfaces.
Write the first line of the class with both interfaces.
Write the fields, the constructor and the four methods, each with public in front.
Take the // off the TourBus lines in main and run the file.
hints: A class has one parent at most, but it can implement as many interfaces as it needs.
After implements, list both interfaces with a comma between them. The class then writes every method of both.
The first line: `class TourBus implements Bookable, Departing {`.

tasks.title: Book a whole trip, or none of it
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class `Trip` with a method `static boolean bookAll(ArrayList<Bookable> parts, int places)`. When every part has that many places free, it books them on each part and gives back `true`. When any part is short, it books nothing at all, on any part, and gives back `false`.

Check runs your class beside a `Bookable` of its own and with bookable parts of its own, which you have never seen, and reads what `bookAll` gives back and how many places each part has free afterwards.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about a method that asks only for an interface.
Write the class and the first line of bookAll exactly as the task gives it.
First find out whether every part has room, without booking anything.
Only then book every part, and take the // off the last lines in main.
hints: bookAll does not need to know what each part is: a bike shed, a bus, or something new. Bookable is enough.
Booking as you go leaves half a trip booked when a later part is short. Use two loops: one that only looks, one that books.
The first loop gives back false as soon as `part.placesFree() < places`; the second calls `part.book(places)` on each part.
